cards.front: Recall a key point about Specialisation and Division of Labour
cards.back: Specialisation means focusing on producing a limited range of goods or services — individuals, firms, and countries can all specialise.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Specialisation and Division of Labour
cards.back: Division of labour breaks production into separate tasks, with each worker performing one task. Adam Smith identified this as a key source of productivity gains.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Specialisation and Division of Labour
cards.back: Benefits: increased productivity, time saved (no switching tasks), specialist equipment, higher output and lower unit costs.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Specialisation and Division of Labour
cards.back: Costs: worker boredom and demotivation, over-dependence on one product or market, skills become obsolete if the industry changes.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Specialisation and Division of Labour
cards.back: Specialisation leads to exchange because no one produces everything they need — workers earn wages from their specialism and buy other goods, creating interdependence.

cards.front: What should you know about economics exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating specialisation, use the PBR framework: Productivity gains, Boredom costs, Resilience (how vulnerable is the specialist to change?).
High skill, higher pay, career progression (e.g. Boredom, deskilling, redundancy risk)
Lower costs, higher efficiency, economies of scale (e.g. Vulnerable to demand shifts in one product)
Export strength, trade surplus in specialism (e.g. Import dependency, sector-specific shocks)
Comparative advantage, greater total output (e.g. Trade disputes, supply chain disruption)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Specialisation always benefits workers because it makes them more productive. Correct: While specialisation increases productivity, it can harm workers: narrowing skills (vulnerability to industry decline), causing monotony, reducing bargaining power. cards.back: AO1 — Knowledge: Demonstrate knowledge of Specialisation and Division of Labour with precise business/economic terminology. Define key terms and state accurate factual information.

cards.front: Specialisation and the Division of Labour
cards.back: Specialisation occurs when individuals, firms or countries concentrate on producing a limited range of goods or services. The division of labour is a specific form of specialisation where a production process is broken down into separate tasks, each performed by a different worker. The main advantages of specialisation are increased productivity, lower average costs, greater efficiency, and higher output. Workers who repeat the same task become faster and more accurate; firms can invest in specialist machinery; and countries can export goods they produce efficiently whilst importing the rest.
